ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
International Air Services From Bangalore 
22I. SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA: Will the Minister of CIVIL 
AVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Bangalore Airport is shortly going to be on 
international airport map; 
(b) whether apart from Nepal Airlines any other international 
airlines is going to have flights from Bangalore; 
(c) if so, the name of other international airlines which are going 
to have flights from Bangalore; and 
(d) whether it will not have adverse effect on finance of domestic 
airlines? 
THE MINISTER OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRI SHARD 
YADAV): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (d) Existing domestic airport at Bangalore has been declared 
as an international airport in May, 2000, During last round of bilateral 
air services consultations with Mala ysia and Gulf Air owning States in 
September. 2000. Bangalore has been granted as an additional point of 
call to Gulf Air and the designated airline of Malaysia. Actual 
operations, however, are left to their commercial judgement. Operations 
of both Gulf Air and designated airline of Malaysia to/from Bangalore 
shall be covered by a Code Share/Block Space agreement with the 
designated airline of India.

Decline in Foreign Exchange Reserves 
*222. SHRI V. P. DURAISAMY: Will the Minister of FINANCE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that India's foreign exchange reserves have 
fallen further by $181 mil'ion to $34,861 million in the week ended 
October 20, 2000 over the previous week; 
7 

RAJYA SABHA [5th December, 2000] 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) what was the reason for decline in foreign exchange reserves; 
and 
(d) what steps Government would take to arrest decline in 
foreign 
exchange reserves'? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI YASHWANT SINHA): 
(a) to (d) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
STATEMENT 
(a) and (b) Yes, Sir. However, the foreign exchange reserves have 
subsequently increased by US $4179 million to US $39,040 million at 
the end of November, 2000. 
(c) Movements in foreign exchange reserves reflect demand-
supply gaps in the foreign exchange market emanating from inflows 
and outflows on account of India's in ternational transactions both on 
the current and capital accounts of balance of payments. Much of the 
excess demand for foreign exchange during this period was attributable 
to the surge in India's oil import bill because of the tripling of 
international oil prices between early 1999 and mid-2000. 
(d) The Government and the Reserve Bank of India monitor 
closely the developments in the balance of payments and in the 
financial markets at home and abroad and take such measures, as are 
considered necessary, from time to lime to increase exports and 
invisible receipts, including remittances, to enhance the inflows of 
capital, particularly foreign direct investments, and to maintain orderly 
conditions in the forgein exchange market. 
SHRI V, P. DURAISAMY. Sir. my first supplementary is this. 
The fact that India's foreign exchange reserves have fallen is a very 
serious matter. We need foreign exchange for importing crude oil and 
other capital goods. If the balance of  payments position is strong, the 
international financial institutions wo uld come forward to give loans, 
and our credit worthiness would increase. Does this mean that the 
reserves have fallen despite the inflow of funds from the State Bank of 
India's India Millennium Deposit Scheme? Does this also  mean that 
the reserves have fallen due to the fall in the Rupee value against the 
US Dollar' The Minister can enlighten this House about this. 
Why is there so much of volatility in the Rupee? Why, is some 
weeks, it is going up: and in some weeks, it is coming down drastically 
in the foreign exchange market ' It is linked to the volatility in the stock 
market? What is its 
8 

[5th December, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
impact on the hike in the international oil prices? According to the RBI 
officials, the fall in the reserves wad due to the depreciation of the 
Euro against the Dollar and the conse quent revaluation of the reserves 
thereof. How far this is correct? 
SHRI YASHWANT SINHA: Sir, the hon. Member has raised a 
number of issues. I will try to answer them one by one. The first one is 
this. I entirely agree with him that we must have a comfortable foreign 
exchange reserves because if we do not have a comfortable foreign 
exchange reserves, then it is very easy for pressures to build up on the 
balance of payments front. 
The second one is that the volatility that we have noticed, in 
recent months, in the exchange market, is ascribable to a number of 
factors; prominently, due to a very steep increase in the international 
petroleum prices, The House, perhaps, is aware that as a result of the 
increase in the international petroleum prices, our annual import bill for 
crude and its products is estimated to be anything between US$17 to US 
$18 billion this year. It is up by about US $7 to US $8 billion, when 
compared to last year. Now, the increase in the international oil prices 
and whatever is happening in the U.S. economy have created volatility 
in the exchange market throughout the world. The Rupee has 
depreciated against the Dollar because the Dollar has been 
strengthening against all currencies, particularly against the Euro and 
the British Pound and, therefore, a certain amount of volatility has been 
noticed in our markets also. The H ouse is aware that, in our country, 
after the Rupee was made convertible on the current account, it is 
freely traded in the exchange market and the value of the Rupees vis-a-
vis the other currencies depends exactly on the laws of supply and 
demand. If the supplies come in and are able to meet the demand, the 
Rupee remains stable. If supplies are less than what the demand is, 
then there is volatility. As I said, as a result of the increase in the oil 
bill, we have noticed a certain volatility in recent months. Now, the RBI, 
which is managing the exchange rate, tries to balance the reserves that 
we have with the volatility in the exchange market and they always try 
and ensure that orderly conditions  prevail in the exchange market. 
Therefore, I think, they have done a good job of this. Despite the fact 
that the entire world has seen volatil ity, in India, we have been able to 
manage the situation very well. We went to the NRI community once 
again with the India Millennium Deposit Scheme. The State Bank of 
India, which went out to all the markets except the U.S. market, was 
able to raise, in about less than a fortnight's time, over US $5.51 
billion and the figures of reserves that I have given of over US $39  
9 

RAJYA SABHA [5th December, 2000] 
billion at the end of November also reflects the receipts under the India 
Millennium Deposit Scheme. We have arrested the decline in the foreign 
exchange reserves. We are comfortably placed and there is absolutely 
nothing to worry on this account. 
SHRI V. P. DURAISAMY: Sir, my second supplementary is, 
generally, when there is an increase in foreign exchange reserves, its 
conversion into rupee by the Reserve Bank of India and loading it in 
the market leads to inflation. Then, why is the inflation at a higher level, 
despite a fall in the foreign exchange reserves? If the position of a 
foreign exchange reserves is satisfactory, has it any thing to do with the 
passing of the FEMA? Is it likely to increase? 
SHRI YASHWANT SINHA: Sir, the rate of inflation, in India, is 
determined by a number of factors. Money supply, especially what is 
called the M-III, has a role to play. Fortunately, the M-III has been 
under control this year. Money expansion has been less than 15 per 
cent — 14.7 per cent, to be precise. As far as the IMD is concerned, the 
Reserve Bank of India has worked out a method by which they will 
mop up the surplus, and will not allow it to impact on money supply in 
the country. But, at the same time, we are also aware that in a country 
like India, where we have a large number of administered prices, any 
revision in administered prices has a direct impact on the price 
situation. For instance, in the curr ent year, we have now an inflation 
rate — week to week — of about 7.5 per cent. The reason: is basically, 
petroleum products in the country, whose prices have been raised by 
the Government, come under the administered price mechanism. That 
is the most important reason for this increase in the rate of inflation. 
The core rate of inflation continues to be hovering around 3 per cent. 
The FEMA has nothing to do with prices.

comfortable with whatever level of reserves they have because, what is

Now, as far as utilisation part is concerned, a part of the money which

DR. BIPLAB DASGUPTA: The hon. Finance Minister has 
made a claim that our foreign exchange reserve is quite satisfactory; 
and it is being properly managed. But, by making this tall claim, are 
we not deceiving the people of India? Becuase the reserve is unstable 
and hollow. If you look at the composition of the foreign exchange 
reserves $ 39 billion, most of it has come not by way of export surplus. 
If you compare with China or Taiwan or Japan, in all these countries, 
the huge resreves that have been accumulating over a time are on the 
basis of export surplus. We have no export surplus becuase of a deficit 
of more than $7 or 8 billion. With th is deficit, whatever we have in the 
form of reserves is unstable. It can disappear in a matter of month. It 
can disappear in the market. Most of the reserves has been built by the 
NRI remittances; by the short-term capital movement of multinational 
companies, FIIs, by black money returning into our country, in vaious 
forms and loans from exchange safe. We have not acheived that so far. 
The reserves that we have is unstable and hollow. It can disappear in 
one month. Could the Minister kindly react to this? 
SHRI YASHWANT SINHA: Mr. Chairman, Sir, partly, I agree 
with the hon. Member, and partly, strongly disagree with him. This 
issue has been raised from time to time. Therefore, this point has to be 
squarely met. Experience has shown, whatever foreign exchange 
reserves we have and the compos ition of those reserves are not 
unstable. 
I would like to empahsise that they are not unstable. If proof is 
needed of this fact, it lies in the r ealisation that at the height of the 
East-Asian crisis, 
15 

RAJYA SABHA [5th December, 2000] 
which was happening in our backyard, so to say, there was no run on 
the reserves of India. If you are talking about the foreign institutional 
investors the withdrawals from In dia were less than four million 
dollars despite all the crisis whic h was happening elsewhere. There 
was no withdrawal of NRI deposits. We continued to add to it. In 
1999- 2000, they came back strongly and, Sir, the fact that I would like 
to make is, in two years, in 1998-99 and 1999-2000, we added 
something like nine billion dollars to our reserves. Why does one add 
to the reserves? One adds to the reserv es exactly in order to be able to 
meet the requirements of a rainy day. When the going is not so food, 
then we have to use our reserves. There is nothing in our experience 
which suggests that the reserves that  we have are unstable, that they 
can finish in one month's time. I do not buy that theory and I would not 
like to subscribe to it at all becaus e it will unnecessarily spread panic 
which we do not need. That is the last thing that we need in this 
country. Our reserves position is co mfortable. We are in a position to 
manage the situation very well. Come what may, I do not think there is 
going to be any run on our currency which we are not capable of 
managing. 
The second point with which I would like to agree is the fact we 
have to build our reserves genuinely, truly, by running down our deficit 
on trade account and ensuring that more capital inflows take place, that 
the current account deposit becomes positive instead of being negatives 
over the years and that we attract more foreign direct investment. That 
is the surest way of having very comfortable reserves and feeling 
absolutely confident about it.

Measures to overcome water crisis in States 
†*235. SHRI RAJ MAHINDER SINGH: 
SHRI RAM JETHMALANI:  
Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that possibilities of further deepening of water 
crisis in several States of the country have been noticed; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the names of such States; 
(c) whether Government have prepared any action plan to provide 
rapid solution to this crisis; and 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
37 
 

RAJYA SABHA 15th December, 2000] 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI ARJUN 
SETHI): (a) to (d) The average annual per capita water availability is 
estimated to be about 1869 cu.m. in 2000 AD at national level. The per 
capital availability is likely to decline to about 1342 Cum by 2025 AD 
due to increase in population. 
Availability of water in rivers is assessed River basin-wise. A per 
the criteria adopted by some international agencies, any situation of 
water availability of less than 1000 Cubic meters per capita per year is 
considered as a scarcity condition. According to this criterion, the 
scarcity situations already exists in eight of the river basins namely: 
Pennar, East flowing rivers between Pennar and Kanyakumari, Cauvery, 
West flowing rivers of Kutch and Saurashtra including Luni, Sabarmati, 
Tapi, Mahi and East flowing rivers between Mahanadi and Godavari. A 
part of Maharashtra state which falls in the Tapi Basin is also therefore 
facing water scarcity. 
Accordingly to India Meteorological Department, the rainfall in 
the country during this year's mons oon has been 8% lower than the 
long-term average for the country as a whole. National Disaster 
Management (NDM) Division of the Ministry of Agriculture has 
mentioned that due to the deficient rains of the South-West monsoon, 
the States of Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Chhatisgarh, Orissa and 
Rajasthan are experiencing the drought-like conditions which may 
intensify in the summer months of the year 2001. 
With a view to provide solution to the likely crisis, the 
Government has taken various short term and long- term measures, 
which include the following: 
Central Water Commission and Ministry of Water Resources 
have advised the State Governments to regulate the releases 
from the reservoirs keeping in view the possible water deficit and 
making curtailment for irrigation in consultation with the State 
Agriculture Departments. 
For promotion of Rain Water Harvesting through Watershed 
Management Programmes, Artificial recharge of Ground 
Water and roof-top rain water harvesting under the Sector 
reform project of Accelarated Rural Water Supply Programme 
under the Ministry of Rural Development, technical and 
financial assistance is provided to the State Governments and 
other implementing agencies. 
The exploratory tube wells drille d by the Central Ground Water 
Board (CGWB) are also transferred to the States for drinking water-
supply. 
For regulation and control of ground water the Central Ground 
Water Board has been constitu ted as an Authority under 
section 3 (3) of the Environment Protection Act, 1986. 
38 

[5th December, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
To ensure regulation of ground wa ter in a scientific manner, the 
Government of India had prepared a Model Bill in 1970, 
subsequently revised in 1992 and circulated to the States for 
enacting legislation. 
National Water Development Agency has formulated National 
Perspective Plan for water resources development, which 
envisages inter-linking between various Peninsular Rivers and 
Himalayan Rivers for transfer of water from surplus basins to 
water deficit basins. 
The Government has taken up Water Resources Consolidation 
Projects with the assistance of World Bank to improve 
efficiency of irrigation waler use in the country and early 
completion of on going schemes. 
Union Government has launched the Accelerated Irrigation 
Benefits Programme (AIBP) since 1996-97 for providing 
Central Loan Assistance to the State Governments for 
completion of those irrigation projects which are in advance 
stages of completion or mega projects which are beyond their 
resources capability.

process consisting of seismic data acquistion, processing, 
interpretation, prospect identification and drilling. Exploration 
process begins with geological and geophysical surveys. The areas thus 
identified are assessed for likely hydrocarbon potential through 
various methods of resource appraisa l; favourable results lead to the 
next state of exploration during which targets are decided and 
prospects identified. Each prospect thus demarcated is evaluated 
techo-economically and the desirability or otherwise of drilling is spelt 
out and priority accorded. 
39 

RAJYA SABHA [5th December, 2000] 
Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Lid. (ONGC) and Oil India Ltd. 
(OIL) are continuing.exploratory activities in the country. Since 
inception upto 1.4.2000, ONGC has acquired 3,11,485 Ground Line

Kilometer (SSK), 39,183 GLK and 67 Square Kilometre (Sq. Km), of 3D 
(three dimensional) seismic data in onland areas, and 5,15,843 Line

(c) if not, the reasons therefor; 
(d) whether Government will take a decision immediately to 
abolish its monopoly for bringing down the prices of petroleum 
products in the country and making their prices competitive; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI E. PONNUSWAMY): (a) to 
(e) Government in November 1997, decided the details of phasing of 
dismantling programme of administered pricing mechanism (APM) for 
moving towards a competitive mark et in the petroleum sector. 
Accordingly, the petroleum sector is scheduled for full deregulation 
from April 2002 onwards. Pursuant to the said decision, the consumer 
prices of all petroleum products except petrol, diesel, ATF, kerosene for 
public distribution system and domestic LPG have been decontrolled 
and the retention pricing system has been abolished for the refineries 
with effect from 1.4.1998. As per the programme, the price of domestic 
LPG is to be suitably adjusted to reach subsidy level at 15% of import 
parity during the year 2000-01. Suitable adjustment in prices of 
kerosene for public distribution would be made to reach subsidy level at 
33.33% of the import parity. On full deregulation, 2002 onwards, the 
subsidy on kerosene for public distribution and LPG domestic will be 
transferred to the fiscal budget of the Government. The domestic 
consumer prices would depend on the oil and product price:, in the 
international market.

Statement-I 
Recommendations of Dr. Nitish Sen Gupta Committee Report 
On the basis of detailed study and assessment of various key 
success factors, the Committee has evaluated and assessed the position of 
IBP, CRL, MRL, BRPL and NRL. Th e Committee has also carefully 
considered the likely status of BPC in the context of a completely 
deregulated scenario. 
Taking into consideration the evaluation and assessment carried out 
by the Committee, the following recommendations have been made so 
as to ensure that all stand-alone o il companies become stronger in the 
deregulated market and also to create a fair and competitive market for 
enhancement of customer services: 
(a) BPC should buy up the entire shareholding of Govt, of India in 
CRL and make CRL its subsidiary. The marketing arrangement, if any, 
with IOC should accordingly be modified. 
(b) Though at present IOC is a st rong candidate for an alliance 
with MRL, the Committee recommends that for the time being the 
marketing arrangement of MRL with IOC should continue. Since, IOC 
is already a dominant player and as it is necessary to ensure fair 
competition, the Committee suggests that BPC be also considered in 
the intermediate future as a serious candidate alongwith IOC to partner 
MRL. However, this should be done after about 18-24 months to allow 
BPC sufficient time to stabilise after its takeover of CRL and the 
demonstration of its ability to do so without affecting the supply line 
and its recommended investment in IBP. 
172 

[5th December, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) IOC should buy up the entire shareholding of Govt, of India in 
BRPL and make this company its subsidiary. 
(d) NRL should continue with BPC and IBP who are the 
majority shareholders along with Government of Assam. However, the 
Committee recommends that OIL should  be roped in as a shareholder 
with 10% share, which can be allotted to them on preferential allotment 
basis out of the shares earmarked for public issue thereby creating an 
inte grated oil net work in the North East. This process will also 
enhance the sentiment of the prospective investors in the capital 
market for purposes of its ensuing public issue. 
(e) The Committee recommends that IBP should continue as a 
separate corporate entity for the time  being. However, it feels that IBP 
needs a strong strategic partner for continued supply of products and 
also providing marketing back up and necessary financial support. 
Accordingly, it endorses the views of the Disinvestment 
Commission mat Government of India should disinvest 33.58% in 
favour of a strategic partner. After careful study and consideration at 
various strategic alliance options, based on various success factors, the 
Committee feels that BPC is a strong candidate in comparison to other 
oil companies. Therefore, Government of India should disinvest its 
shareholdings in IBP in excess of 26% in favour of BPC as permissible 
under the SEBI take over guidelines. If these guidelines stand in the 
way of one shot of acquisition of this block of shareholding by BPC, 
this may have to be done in phases or a portion of the shareholding now 
held by financial institutions may have to be transferred to BPC. 
(f) IBP should be assured of the required products from Mathura 
and/or Panipat in the North and MRL and CRL in the South through 
appropriate marketing tie-ups for a pe riod of at least five years after 
the end of APM period in order to maintain its supplies. 
(g) Government of India should constitute a petroleum regulatory 
body in lieu of OCC, who should regulate the supply of products 
besides handing critical issues during the transition period of 
deregulation. 
(h) All the existing pipelines excl uding strategic pipelines owned 
by IOC should be transferred to an independent company such as the 
Petronet India Limited so that all the marketing companies get fair and 
equitable access to these pipelines for movement of products.

European Union to agree to the relaunch of a new round of negotiation

(c) if not, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (SHRI OMAR ABDULLAH): (a) to (c) In their 
Interaction with India at various levels, the European Union has been 
waking India's endorsement to the launch of a new round of negotiations 
under the WTO with a comprehensive agenda. A similar effort was 
made by European Union and other developed countries during the 
preparations for, and in, the Third Ministerial Conference of WTO at 
Seattle, USA in November-December 1999. As the discussions at the 
Third Ministerial Conference of WT O at Seattle were inconclusive,

new round of negotiations other than the mandated negotiations as have 
been provided under the various WTO agreements. 
India is not in favour of overloading the WTO agenda with wide-
ranging new round of negotiations and is, in any case opposed to 
adding of new non-trade issues on the WTO agenda such as core labour 
standards, environmental issues, coherent global architecture, 
investment, competition policy and involvement of non-governmental 
organisations in negotiations. India is, however, prepared for a few new 
items being taken up for negotiations, provided the implementation 
issues arising from the Uruguay Round are also resolved to its 
satisfaction.

Advertising Policy of the Government of India 
"A" Preamble:

publication concerned are not taken into account. However,

(d) to what extent process of disinvestment has taken place; and 
(e) by when the disinvestment process of IA and AI is likely to 
be completed? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE DEPARTMENT OF 
DISINVESTMENT, MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
PLANNING. MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
STATISTICS AND PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION AND 
MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF 
ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS AND PUBLIC GRIEVANCES OF 
THE MINISTRY OF PERSONNEL, PUBLIC GRIEVANCES AND 
PENSIONS (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) to (e) In order to maintain 
transparency in the disinvestment process for strategic sale, the 
general procedure being followed is as under: 
• P ropo sal s for Disinvestment in any PSU based on the 
recommendations of the Disinvestment Commission or in 
accordance with the declared Disinvestment Policy of the 
Government, are placed for consideration of the Cabinet 
Committee on Disinvestment (CCD). 
• Alter CCD clears the Disinvestment Proposal, selection of 
the Advisor is done through Competitive Bidding Process. 
• The Advisor assists the Governme nt in preparation and issue 
of advertisement in leading newspapers inviting the 
Expression of Interest (EOI) offers from interested parties. 
• After receipt of the EOIs, Prospective Bidders are short listed 
based on objective screening in the light of announced 
criteria/ requirements. 
• The Advisors, after due dilligence of the PSU, prepare the 
Information memorandum in consultation with the concern 
PSU. This is given to the short listed prospective Bidders 
who have entered into a Confidentiality Agreement. 
• The draft Share Purchase Agreement and the Shareholder 
Agreement are also prepared by the Advisors with the help of 
the Legal Advisors. 
• The Prospective Bidders undertake due diligence of the PSU 
and hold discussions with th e Advisors/the Government/the 
Representatives of the PSU for any clarifications. 
221 

RAJYA SABHA [5th December, 2000] 
• Concurrently the task of valuation of the PSU is undertaken in 
accordance with the standard national and international practices. 
• Based on the reactions received from the Prospective Bidders, the 
Share Purchase Agreement and Shareholders Agreement are 
prepared. After getting them vetted by the Ministry of Law, they are 
approved by the Government. Thereafter, they are sent to the 
Prospective Bidders for inviting the final binding bids (Technical 
and Financial). 
• After examination, analysis and evaluation, the recommendations 
of the Inter Ministerial Group (IMG) are placed before the CCD 
for final decision regarding selection of the Strategic Partner, signing 
of the Share Purchase Agreement and Shareholders Agreement, 
and other ancillary issues. 
• In the disinvestment process mentioned above, Department of 
Disinvestment is assisted at each stage by an Inter Ministerial Group 
(IMG) comprising officers from the Ministry of Finance, Department 
of Public Enterprises, the Administrative Ministry/Department 
controlling the PSU, apart from the officers of the Department of 
Disinvestment and the Advisors. 
• After the transaction is completed all papers and documents relating 
to it shall be turned over to the Comptroller and Auditor General of 
India; the CAG shall prepare an evaluation for sending to Parliament 
and releasing to the public. 
As regards the status of disinvestment process in Indian Airlines and Air 
India, the position is as under: 
• Advertisements in leading newspapers issued on 2.10.2000 inviting 
offers for Expression of Interest (EOI) for Air India and on 29.9.2000 
for Indian Airlines. 
• Advisors for the transactions have received Expression of Interest 
offers from certain prospective partners. 
• The finalization of documents forming part of the Bid Pack, such as 
Information Memorandum, Initial Draft Share Purchase and 
Shareholders Agreements etc., is underway. 
• No final time frame for completing the transaction can be given at 
this stage as the same would depend on various factors like time 
222

taken for the dilligence by the prospective bidders, 
finatization of agreements etc.

1510. SHRI GHULAM NABI AZAD: Will the Minister of

home

THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING 
(SHRIMATI SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) The broad details of the policy on Direct-to-Home 
broadcasting are given in the Statement. 
Statement 
Broad details for establishment, maintenance and operation of direct-
to-home (DTH) Broadcasting service. 
(i) The applicant company shall be an Indian company, registered 
under the Indian Companies Act, 1956. 
(ii) The total Foreign Investment,* including FDI/NRI/OCB/FII 
in the DTH Broadcasting sector, shall not be more than 49%, 
in which the share of FDI will not exceed 20%. 
Provided that the quantum represented by that proportion of 
the paid up equity share capital to the total issued equity 
capital of the Indian promoter Company held or controlled by 
foreign investors through FDI/NRI/OCB investments shall 
form part of the above said FDI limit of 20%. 
No Broadcasting Company and/or Cable Network Company 
shall be eligible to own more than 20% of the total equity of 
an applicant Company at any time during the License period. 
Provided further that the Licensee, at all times, shall keep the 
Licensor informed of any change in the holding pattern of the 
Equity. 
(iii) The applicant company must have Indian management 
control with majority representatives on the Board, as well as 
the CEO of the Company being a resident Indian citizen. 
289 

RAJYA SABHA [5th December, 2000] 
(iv) There will be no restriction on the number of licensees and the 
license will be issued by the Government for a period of 10 years, on 
non-exclusive basis. 
(v) The applicant company shall be required to pay an entry fee of Rs. 
10 crores, in the beginning. In addition, 10% per year of the revenue 
collected by the platform owner from channels shall be payable to 
Government as annual fee. The licensee would also be required to 
execute a Bank guarantee of Rs. 40 crore valid for the duration of 
the licence. Licensee will additionally be required to pay the license 
fee and royalty for spectrum used, as prescribed by the Wireless 
Planning Coordination authority (WPC), under the department of 
Telecommunications. 
(vi) The Licensing Authority shall have the power, after recording the 
reasons in writing, to revoke/ suspend the license in public interest. 
However before taking such action the licensing authority will 
give the licensee an opportunity of being heard. The decision of the 
licensing authority shall be final. 
(vii) For violation of license conditions, in addition to any other action 
which may include revocation of license, a penalty upto Rs. 50 crores 
can be imposed by the Licenser on the Licensee. However, before 
taking such action the licensing authority will give the licensee an 
opportunity of being heard. The decision of the licensing authority 
shall be final. 
Note: * Approvals for foreign equity shall be routed through the FIPB route. 
(viii) The licensee shall establish the uplink Earth Station in India within 12 
months from the date of issue of license. All Content provided by the 
DTH platform to the subscribers, irrespective of its source, to pass 
through the common encryption and conditional access system, located 
within the Earth Station, situated on Indian soil. 
(ix) The licensee shall ensure adherence to the Programme Code (PC) 
and Advertisement Code (AC), laid down by the Ministry of 
Information and Broadcasting, from time to time. Record of the 
programmes and advertisements carried on the platform to be kept 
by the Licensee for a period of 90 days after broadcast and to be 
made available to the authorised representative of the Licenser, as 
and when required. 
290 

[5th December, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(x) The licensee shall provide access to various content providers/ 
channels on a non-discriminatory basis. The licensee shall not carry 
any channels prohibited by the Ministry of I&B. 
(xi) Licensee shall provide access to the Licensing Authority or its duly 
authorised representative, to all its facilities including equipments, 
records, systems, etc. 
(xii) Though licensee can use the bandwidth capacity for DTH service 
on both Indian as well as foreign satellites, proposals envisaging 
use of Indian satellites will be extended preferential treatment. 
(xiii) The licensee shall ensure subscriber's interests through Single 
Conditional Access Technology, Single Subscriber Management 
System (SMS), an Open Architecture (Non-proprietary) Set Top 
Box, a Cast Iron Encryption System and an efficient, responsive and 
accurate billing and collection system. The Licenser shall not use 
any equipment, which is identified as unlawful. 
(xiv) The Licenser reserves the right to prohibit the transmission or 
reception of programmes in the interest of national security or in 
the event of emergency/war or similar type of situation. 
Notwithstanding any agreement between the licensee and the 
content providers, the licensee shall stop forthwith, transmission of 
TV channels or any content, as and when directed to do so by the 
Licenser or any other designated lawful authority. 
(xv) The DTH facility shall no t be used for other modes of 
communication, including voice, fax, data, communication Internet, etc. 
unless specific license for these value-added services has been 
obtained from the competent authority. 
(xvi) The licensee shall obtain clearances/approvals, as may be prescribed 
or required, from the Wireless Planning Coordination Wing or from 
the Department of Space. 
(xvii) The DTH Licensee will be bound to carry channels of Prasar Bharati on 
the most favourable financial terms offered to any other channel. 
(xviii) The Licenser reserves the right to modify or incorporate new 
conditions at any time in the terms and conditions of this license, as 
and when necessary in public interest or interest of national 
security. 
291 

RAJYA SABHA [5th December, 2000] 
(xix) The licensees will adhere to provisions of any legislation 
which may be brought in future with regard to broadcasting.

Order to catch performing animals used by Kalandars 
1532. SHRI RAJNATH SINGH "SURYA": Will the Minister of 
SOCIAL JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have ordered catching of performing 
animals used by the Kalandars; 
(b) if so, whether the order has been complied with; 
(c) whether any alternative source of livelihood has been offered 
to them; and 
(d) if so, what are those? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SOCIAL 
JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT (SHRIMATI MANEKA 
GANDHI): (a) and (b) The exhibition of animals for the purpose of 
entertainment is a cruelty inflicte d on animals and as such is an 
offence under Section 11 of the Prev ention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 
1960 (59 of 1960). This Ministry vide Notification dated 14th October 
1998 has banned five (5) animals viz. bears, monkeys tigers, panthers 
and lions for exhibition and training as performing animals. Whenever 
any instance of violation of provisions of the aforesaid Act/ 
Notification by anyone including Kalandars is brought to the notice of 
this Ministry or any state wildlife departments, the concerned officials 
take appropriate action. 
(c) and (d) Representations have been received from the 
representatives of the Kalandars for their rehabilitation. Suitable 
proposals are being discussed with the representatives of the Kalandars 
for sanctioning loans for income generating schemes through the 
Corporations functioning under this Ministry and also for their 
vocational training and educational support under various schemes run 
by this Ministry. The Ministry has been very prospective in this 
regard.

Modernization of Government Press, Ring Road, New Delhi 
1582. SHRI S. RAMACHANDRAN PILLAI: Will the Minister of 
URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether the modernisation/replacement of ageing and 
technologically obsolete machines, which have become most essential, 
is sporadic in 
356 

[5th December, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
Government Presses and efforts to modernise the Press at Ring Road, 
New Delhi, even after sanction in September, 1993 has not succeeded; 
(b) whether the depreciation fund to finance modernisation efforts 
is not operational in any of the presses and the cost of printing is found 
to be higher in Government Presses compared to the rates of private 
presses; 
(c) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(d) the steps being taken by Government in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND 
POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI JAGMOHAN): (a) Out of 21 
Govt, of India Presses, 16 have been modernised/partially modernised 
by inducting offset technology. There has been improvement in the 
quality of printing as well as capacity utilisation after modernisation of 
the Govt, of India Press, Ring Road, new Delhi in 1997. 
(b) and (c) The Depreciation Funds for renewal and replacement 
of machinery in the Govt, of India Presses are not operational at 
present. 
The reasons for high cost of printing in the Govt, of India Presses 
in comparison to private Presses are as under:—  
(i) Government Presses do not function as commercial 
establishments but play the role of model employer providing 
facilities like conveyance allowa nce, dearness allowance etc. 
to its employees as per instructions. 
(ii) Regular expenditure is incu rred on maintaining all facilities 
and complying with satutory Govt, regulations as under the 
Factory Act and other Govt, orders. 
(iii) Overhead expenses are comparatively higher.  
(iv) Presses have to print/execute all types of jobs including short 
run jobs although such jobs are not economical. 
(v)   Absence of competitive technology in Govt, of India Presses. 
(vi)  Interruption in power supply resulting in low production. 
(vii) Mismatch of operatives with reference to machines. 
(d) The steps being taken in this regard arc as follows:—  
(i)    Client Ministries/Departments are being requested to supply 
357 

RAJYA SABHA [5th December, 2000] 
camera-ready copies of manuscripts so that high cost of 
composing by old technology is avoided. 
(ii) Steps are being taken to properly utilize the machines and 
equipment with a view to remove the mismatch between the 
crew and the machine. 
Low capacity utilization of printing presses 
1583. SHRI S. RAMACHANDRAN PILLAI: Will the Minister 
of URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the av erage capacity utilisation varied 
between 31 per cent and 44 per ce nt during 1993-94 and 1997-98 and 
the percentage of utilisation was only 15 to 17 in three presses, besides 
low productivity in all the presses; 
(b) whether the significant delays of over five years in completion 
of jobs and delays of 5-12 years in despatch of printed products were 
another stigma for management inef fectiveness, which had caused late 
receipts of printing costs; 
(c) if, so, what are the reasons therefor; and 
(d) what sincere steps Government propose to take to remove and 
check these deficiencies on a permanent basis? 
THE MINISTER OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND 
POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI JAGMOHAN): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) There has been delay in execution and despatch of 
printed jobs and reasons for the same are as under:—  
(i) Printed material could not be despatched timely due to non-
availability of railway wagons etc. and bills regarding 
printing charges could not be preferred as they are received 
only after supply of the printed material to the indentors. 
(ii) Delay in execution of printed jobs are mainly due to over-
riding priorities given to different jobs by the indentors, delay 
in approval of proofs by the indentors, non-supply of 
complete material/ manuscript by the indentors, old 
machinery and power failure, mismatch of staff with 
machinery, voluminous and long-run jobs, mostly manual 
system of binding and other similar limitations. 
358 

[5th December, 2000] RAJYA SABHA

under:—  
(i) Close monitoring through progress reports from the Presses 
for getting the pending jobs completed in a time bound 
manner. 
(ii) The indenting Ministries/Departments have been requested to 
furnish camera ready copies of manuscripts to avoid delay in 
proof reading. 
(iii) Presses have been instructed  to despatch printed material 
through road transport if railway wagons are not available. 
(iv) Indenting Ministries/Departments have also been requested to 
collect the printed material from the presses, whenever 
possible.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI OMAR ABDULLAH): Sir, I 
move the following Motion: - 
"That in pursuance of clause (c) of sub-section (3) of 
Section 4 of the Marine Products Export Development 
Authority Act, 1972 (13 of 1972) read with sub-rule 2 of

Authority Rules, 1972, this House do proceed to elect in

from the membership of Rajya Sabha on July 1, 2000". 
The question was put and the motion was adopted.
